tools.name: runledger
tools.description: Open an agent session like a file and see where the tokens actually went. The idea file's premise was inverted by measurement before a line was written: it framed repeated content as an anomaly to hunt, but pricing 25 real sessions per model against the published 2026-08-09 rate card gives cache READS 73.2% of the bill ($749.26 of $1,023.47) against 15.0% cache write, 11.7% output and 0.1% uncached input. Repetition is not the anomaly, it IS the bill, so the product is a CARRY-COST LEDGER: every row is a turn, showing what it added and how many later turns re-read it. (1) THE ARITHMETIC IS EXACT, NOT ESTIMATED, AND NO TOKENIZER SHIPS. The spec called for gpt-tokenizer (o200k_base, ~2 MB) plus @huggingface/tokenizers; both were cut. cache_read(N) IS the previous turn's prompt — measured over 12,475 turn pairs from 80 real sessions the residual has a median of exactly 2 tokens (a fixed cache-breakpoint offset, not an error) and lands within +/-64 for 96.9%. So input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens is already the EXACT token count of everything appended since the previous turn, and a tokenizer would replace a true number with an estimate of it. There is no public local Anthropic tokenizer anyway, so a tiktoken figure labelled Claude would be a fabrication. (2) THE FIRST IMPLEMENTATION DROPPED UNRECONCILED TURNS AND WAS MEASURABLY WRONG. Discarding them breaks the p_i = p_(i-1) + d_i chain either side of the gap: coverage of the reported cache-read column fell to 78.25% on a session with 9 resets in 29 turns and 83.61% on one with 19 in 109. They are now SEGMENT BOUNDARIES reported as context resets — the cache expired and the whole context was paid for again at write prices, which in the shipped sample is the single most expensive line at 38.2% of the run. Adding the segment head's own cache read closed the last gap: coverage across 40 real sessions is now min 100.00%, median 100.05%, max 100.09%, and the tool PRINTS that figure rather than asking to be believed. (3) PER-ITEM PRICING WAS REFUSED OUTRIGHT. Calibrating bytes-per-token against the sessions' own ground truth gives a session-level ratio spanning 0.45 to 11.45 (within-session per-turn p25-p75 1.88-4.26), and only 25.6% of turns have one block accounting for 80% of their bytes, so splitting a turn's exact token count between its blocks by size would be a fabrication wearing a decimal point. The ledger's unit is the turn; repeats are reported in BYTES and never in dollars. (4) MINHASH WAS OVER-ENGINEERING BY THREE ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE. The spec wanted 64-bit MinHash over 5-gram shingles with LSH banding; measured blocks per session are median 466, p90 1,197, max 1,230, at which a plain Map costs microseconds. Exact repeats are 4.4% of appended bytes (1,424,785 of 32,642,318 across 20 large sessions) — a real secondary finding, not the headline it was specified to be. No near-duplicate pass ships: the obvious near-duplicate is the same file re-read after an edit, which is the job, not waste. (5) THE HEADLINE PROMISE WAS UNANSWERABLE AND WAS CUT. Naming 'which MCP server's schema block was re-sent fourteen times' cannot be done: the schemas, the system prompt and CLAUDE.md are not in the log. What ships is the honest partial — the block is sized EXACTLY (median 61,373 tokens before the user's first word across 118 sessions; p25 52,186, p75 81,836, max 107,958), priced exactly, and never itemised; MCP attribution comes from attributionMcpServer/attributionMcpTool, which the records do carry (257 of 1,823 files). A CI honesty gate walks every user-facing string and every generated headline and fails on any claim of schema visibility, negation-aware so it does not fire on the disclaimer itself. (6) TWO REAL BUGS WERE CAUGHT BY THE TESTS, ONE OF THEM A 3x OVERCHARGE. The obvious model regex /opus-4(?:[-.]1)?(?:[^0-9]|$)/ MATCHES claude-opus-4-8, because the next character is a hyphen — silently pricing every current Opus session on the retired Opus 4.1 card at $15/$75 instead of $5/$25. A minor-version parser ships instead, with a run of six or more digits read as a release date rather than a version, and every real model id pinned by test. Zero compaction records exist across all 1,823 files, so compaction handling was cut as unreachable code. Also verified in the browser rather than asserted: all four modals and the drawer pass all four dismissal exits at 375px with real touch-type PointerEvents (26/26), 44x44 hit areas, no sideways scroll, and a full analysis issues requests for the page's own assets and nothing else. 75 tests, zero runtime dependencies.
browser_apis: File.stream() + a first-party NDJSON framer with a carry buffer and a STREAMING TextDecoder — the carry buffer is the whole point (records average kilobytes, so one straddles a chunk boundary constantly, and splitting each chunk independently loses one record per chunk), and the streaming decode is what stops a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence split across a boundary decoding to U+FFFD on both sides. Verified by replaying a document at EVERY chunk size from 1 byte upward

Transferable ReadableStreams into a module Web Worker — the stream is transferred, never copied, so a 500 MB file never enters the worker's heap. Only aggregates cross back: no line, block or file content is ever posted to the main thread

Turn assembly keyed on requestId, NOT on the record — one request emits a thinking block, a text block and one line per tool call, all carrying the SAME usage object (measured: 452 records, 233 assistant records, 83 requests), so per-record summing reports a bill ~2.8x the real one

A segment/suffix-sum carry model: Sum(read_j) = (T-1)*p_1 + Sum(d_i*(T-i)) within a segment, with per-turn cache-read rates carried in a suffix array so a mid-session model switch is priced at the rate actually charged

Exact per-turn pricing from three signals the log carries and competitors ignore: model, usage.speed (fast mode is a flat $10/$50 replacement card on Opus 5/4.8, not a multiplier) and usage.inference_geo (us = 1.1x on EVERY bucket including cache reads), plus the ephemeral_5m/ephemeral_1h split so a 1-hour write is charged at 2x rather than 1.25x

First-party 128-bit content hash (two FNV-1a passes with different bases) — Web Crypto SHA-256 was rejected on purpose: it is async, which would infect every function touching a block, and its only advantage is collision resistance against an adversary who here would be the user colliding two blocks of their own log

DataTransferItem.webkitGetAsEntry with a LOOPED readEntries (it returns at most 100 at a time and says nothing when it stops), plus showDirectoryPicker {mode:'read'} feature-detected and never persisted, offered only as a labelled desktop convenience because Chrome refuses sensitive locations and ~/.claude is invisible in the macOS dialog without Cmd+Shift+period

First-party RFC 4180 CSV writer — control characters become visible escapes so one row is always one physical line, formula-injection guard on =+-@ leads WITH forced quoting (unquoted, some importers strip the apostrophe and restore the formula), ';' quoting for de/fr/es Excel, UTF-8 BOM and CRLF

A self-contained run-report.html built with no script, no link and no src, asserted by test — and asserted by a second test to contain no line of the session: the artefacts carry token counts, tool names and short labels only

Build-output gates run in CI with the build BEFORE the tests so they cannot silently skip: no indexedDB / getDirectory / sessionStorage / document.cookie anywhere in dist/** (dist/** and not dist/assets/**, because generateSW emits sw.js and workbox-<hash>.js at the dist ROOT), exactly two localStorage keys checked as STRING LITERALS because minification hoists the keys into single-letter variables and the obvious call-site regex passes vacuously, no console.* survivors, and both third-party origins named in both CSP directives

tools.name: leakmap
tools.description: Drop in your .env and your dist/ folder and find out which of your secrets your build actually contains — searched byte for byte against your own values rather than a list of known key formats, with any shipped sourcemaps decoded back into your source tree. Seven independent research lenses were run on the original spec and each was refuted by an independent verifier; THIRTY-FIVE corrections came out of it and the load-bearing ones inverted the design. (1) THE HEADLINE CLAIM WAS FALSE. "Exact matching gives zero false positives" fails in both directions, and the matcher is innocent in both. Searching all 43 values of a realistic .env over 5.05 MB of real production bundles produced 76,738 MATCH EVENTS: `1` -> 37,781, `en` -> 37,488, `30` -> 1,786, `dark` -> 271, `true` -> 97. Length is not the discriminator either — random [a-z0-9] strings average 0.020 hits at length 4 and 0.000 at length >=5, while dictionary-shaped `function` (8 chars) gets 9,303. SHAPE predicts noise, so an 8-rung gate ships, every rung carrying a displayed reason and a per-variable override, plus a post-hoc demotion on the REAL hit count (never a predicted one: N/A^L is off by nine orders of magnitude on dictionary words). (2) IT ALSO INHERITS GREP'S RECALL — 9/14. Measured on a real Vite 8.2.1 build, `grep -rF` found 9 of 14 planted values and a byte-exact matcher found the same 9, hit for hit. The misses were mundane: a backslash, `</script>` (escaped to `<\/script>` in every quote context), a tab, U+2028, a multi-line PEM. Escape-variant enrolment takes it to 14/14 for +4 to +8 patterns. Two sub-corrections: the `\xNN` fear is WRONG for Vite, which hard-sets esbuild charset:"utf8" so `sénhã-très-£42` ships verbatim; and Vite 8 defaults to BACKTICK quoting, where `"` and `'` are not escaped at all. (3) VITE 8 DOES NOT USE DOTENV. It imports parseEnv from node:util, and the two parsers disagree on real input — measured on node v22, `"A=   \nB=b\n"` gives dotenv {A:"",B:"b"} but parseEnv {A:"B=b"}, fabricating one needle and DESTROYING another. Both run and the UNION becomes the needle set, never the intersection: a superfluous needle costs one pattern in a flat-cost automaton, a missing one is a silent false clean. (4) THE VALUE IN THE FILE IS NOT THE VALUE IN THE BUNDLE. Vite runs dotenv-expand and has shipped three different engines; `prefix-${VITE_STRIPE_PK}-suffix` ships expanded, and `tok_dollarX${_NOPE}Y_end` ships MUTATED. All three engines run and every distinct output is enrolled. Separately, .env.production.local beats .env — a tool reading one file reports a false negative on the live value and a false positive on the stale one. (5) THE SOURCEMAP DOES NOT TELL YOU WHERE A BUILD-INLINED SECRET CAME FROM. Measured three ways: with import.meta.env the mapping resolves to a line reading `const key = import.meta.env.VITE_STRIPE_KEY` in which the leaked literal appears nowhere; with the minifier inlining consts it resolved to `src/live.js:6:10 = return [a,b].join("|")` — A DIFFERENT FILE, confidently wrong. Two finding classes ship with different wording, and build-inlined findings are attributed by variable name instead. (6) THE ACCUMULATOR RESET IS THE BUG THAT SHIPS. Per ECMA-426 only the generated column resets at a ';'; sourceIndex, originalLine, originalColumn and nameIndex persist for the whole file. Measured against @jridgewell/sourcemap-codec on a 43-line unminified map, the wrong rule first diverges at generated line 33 and produces 11 NEGATIVE columns — and it is INVISIBLE on a minified single-line bundle, which has no semicolons at all, so it would have shipped green. A free canary asserts non-negativity after every segment. Both candidate libraries were disqualified by measurement rather than preference: @jridgewell/sourcemap-codec@1.5.5 SILENTLY PROMOTES malformed 2- and 3-field segments to [0,0,0,0], fabricating an attribution to sources[0]:1:0, and source-map@0.8.0 CRASHES on an out-of-range index. Also: 7 VLQ groups is legal, not 6 (2^31-1 encodes as "+/////D"), and "B" decodes to -0 unless normalised. (7) SOURCEMAP COLUMNS ARE UTF-16 CODE UNITS, NOT BYTES. Measured on a real vite@8.2.1 build, an 824-byte / 794-UTF-16-unit file put the needle at byte 766 = UTF-16 736 — a delta of THIRTY from a handful of emoji. Using the byte offset as a column shifts every finding after the first non-ASCII character by a constant, which looks internally consistent while being uniformly wrong. The raw byte offset is always printed beside the mapped location so a bad mapping is visible rather than confident. (8) FINDING SOURCEMAPS ONE WAY GIVES A GREEN REPORT OVER A REAL LEAK. Globbing `*.map` misses `--sourcemap inline` (zero .map files, whole map embedded); scanning contents misses `--sourcemap hidden` (map on disk, comment stripped). leakmap takes the union of three paths and treats an orphan map as a HIGHER-severity finding. The naive comment regex is a confident-wrong-answer machine: a planted decoy string literal wins over the real trailing comment, the spec's own anchored body pattern returns NULL on every block-comment/CSS map because `\s*` does not trim the closer, a BOM defeats `^` entirely, and U+2028 IS a line terminator to the m flag. Real Vite emits `data:application/json;charset=utf-8;base64,` — a parser matching the spec's literal `;base64` finds nothing. (9) AN INDEX MAP READS AS CLEAN. It has no top-level mappings, sources or sourcesContent, so `(map.mappings||'').split(';')` yields zero segments and a clean report WHILE THE MAP PUBLISHES THE ENTIRE SOURCE TREE. Array.isArray(map.sections) is tested first, before any other field; the original line number is refused loudly (offset.column applies only when innerLine===0, so a half-correct decoder shifts every line silently) while sourcesContent is still recovered. (10) THE HIGHEST-SEVERITY FINDING NEEDS NO SEARCH AT ALL: a .env copied into public/ ships verbatim as dist/.env, and that is a filename check. The sample proves it live — every variable in it becomes public, including DB_PASSWORD, which no bundler would ever have inlined. (11) `../../src/main.js` IS THE ORDINARY VITE SHAPE, NOT AN ATTACK. A path guard that rejects every `..` is trivially 'safe' and made source recovery produce NOTHING on every normal build; the unit tests missed it because they had encoded the same wrong rule, and the end-to-end run over a real build caught it. Leading `..` is dropped (capped at four), `..` after a real segment is refused rather than popped. fflate sanitises nothing and the OS unzipper honours `../`, so the boundary has to be here. (12) FOUR DOWNLOADS FROM ONE GESTURE TRIPS CHROME'S LIMITER on every user — the second programmatic download flips to PROMPT_BEFORE_DOWNLOAD and, if the bubble is missed, artefacts two to four silently never arrive. One artefact per explicit click. (13) LAST-4 MASKING IS WRONG FOR THREE SHAPES: last-4 of a DATABASE_URL is `5432`, of a PEM block is `KEY-`, and for a 9-character value it is 44% of the secret. A shape-aware ladder ships, suffix-only, capped at 25%, applied unconditionally including to public-by-design values — a uniform mask is what stops a later refactor printing the 'safe' ones in full and, one condition inversion later, the unsafe ones. There is no reveal control anywhere in the product. (14) `frame-ancestors` IS INERT IN A META POLICY (CSP3, normative) and GitHub Pages cannot set headers, so it is deliberately absent and six lines of real JS framebusting ship instead — the threat model must not claim what the code does not do. Supabase's sb_secret_/sb_publishable_ keys are now first-class rules, because a JWT-only implementation in 2026 misses the exact critical finding; and `AIza` is classified by NEIGHBOURHOOD, since a Firebase key (which Google says is safe to publish), a Maps key and a Gemini key are indistinguishable from the string alone. Verified in the browser rather than asserted: a full run over the sample issues requests for the page's own assets and NOTHING else; all five overlays pass all four dismissal exits at 375px with real touch-type PointerEvents; and none of the nine planted secrets appears in any of the four artefacts. 194 tests. GitHub's own push protection rejected the first push over leakmap's sample .env — the sample now carries a key one detail off a real one, and says why.
browser_apis: First-party dense-table Aho-Corasick over BYTES (one Int32Array(256) goto row per node, fail links folded in) — chosen on pattern count and streaming, NOT raw speed: measured, AC is flat at 362-378 MB/s regardless of P while indexOf is ~4x faster at P=5, with the crossover between P=5 and P=20. After expansion-union and variant enrolment a 15-secret .env yields 40-90 patterns, past the crossover. Matching on bytes is provably safe rather than convenient: UTF-8 is self-synchronising, verified exhaustively over a dense sample of the whole scalar range with zero non-boundary matches — and decoding first would be actively wrong, since a non-fatal TextDecoder substitutes U+FFFD and shifts every later offset

tools.name: charsight
tools.description: Find the characters in a file that your screen will not show you, read what they say, and get the file back byte-identical except what you approved. Adversarial verification refuted several load-bearing pieces of the design and every correction changed the build. (1) THE OBVIOUS EMOJI RULE IS 86% WRONG. "A zero-width joiner flanked by Extended_Pictographic is legitimate" misclassifies 1,391 of Unicode 17's own 1,614 RGI emoji ZWJ sequences, because the characters actually adjacent to the joiner are usually a skin-tone modifier (Emoji_Modifier) or U+FE0F (a variation selector) and neither is Extended_Pictographic. Charsight steps outward past that glue first, which takes the misclassification to zero. (2) SCRIPT CONTEXT MUST BE LOCAL, NOT DOCUMENT-WIDE. A zero-width non-joiner between two Arabic-script letters is orthographically required whether the document is Persian or an English README quoting one Persian word — the document-level test stripped it out of the shipped sample, which is the commonest real case. (3) AN INVISIBLE CHARACTER MUST NOT VOTE ON THE DOCUMENT'S SCRIPT: U+3164 HANGUL FILLER is Script=Hangul, so in `user<filler>name` the one invisible character is 11% of the text, Hangul becomes "dominant", and the finding argues itself down to a plausible Korean jamo filler. (4) HTML-ESCAPING IS THE WRONG THREAT MODEL FOR THE ARTEFACTS. It stops < and & and does nothing to U+202E, so a report quoting a bidi payload verbatim reorders its own prose in the reader's browser — the file you attach to a security ticket, Trojan-Sourced by the one tool that knows better. One rendering path chips every invisible and reordering code point BEFORE it reaches a DOM or a file, and the lossless form is the hex dump beside it. (5) THE BYTE-EXACTNESS CHECK EVERYONE WRITES IS A TAUTOLOGY. Comparing untouched byte ranges can only fail if memcpy is broken. The real failure: charsight passes ill-formed bytes through untouched by design, so deleting a well-formed span sitting BETWEEN two ill-formed fragments joins them into a brand-new valid code point that was in neither the input nor any finding — no byte altered, the file now says something different. Verified by re-decoding the output and comparing against what the policy predicted; a test reproduces the exact case. (6) Default_Ignorable_Code_Point is the obvious master list and is wrong in both directions — half of it is essential to some language, and it explicitly subtracts White_Space, which excludes the unusual spaces that are the commonest reason people arrive. (7) getTextContent() CANNOT BE USED FOR PDFs: pdf.js deletes every \p{Cf} character — every zero-width, every bidi control, the whole tag block — and flattens NBSP to a space, in BOTH normalisation modes, so a check built on it reports every poisoned PDF as clean. The text is rebuilt from getOperatorList showText glyph arrays instead, per-run gated on whether the font has a usable character map. (8) RENDER MODE 3 IS ALSO HOW EVERY SCANNED PDF CARRIES ITS OCR LAYER, so the mechanism is named rather than scored. (9) A numeric severity column in findings.csv is an invitation to sort typography two rows below a smuggled instruction on one scale of suspicion, so the column is an unrankable slug. Also corrected in build: pdf.js 6 removed isEvalSupported (the v4 incantation the rest of the fleet uses no longer type-checks); the table generator joined its string tables on a literal backslash-n, so every .split('\n') returned one element and the entire confusables map and name lookup silently returned nothing — caught by a test, not by reading. THE HONESTY GATE IS ENFORCED BY CI: a test walks every user-facing string, every category description, the note shipped with the artefacts and every finding from a real scan, and fails on any claim about who or what wrote the text; exactly one constant is exempt, by name. It caught a real violation on its first run. 258 tests.
browser_apis: First-party UTF-8/UTF-16 decoder yielding {codePoint, byteOffset, byteLength, line, column} in ONE pass — strict per RFC 3629, so overlong forms, encoded surrogates and anything above U+10FFFF are reported as invalid bytes rather than decoded. TextDecoder cannot be used: it substitutes U+FFFD for every invalid byte, so a file with one Windows-1252 byte decodes to something that is not on disk and any 'cleaned' output silently corrupts bytes nobody asked to touch

First-party byte splicer — detection reads a decoded COPY, the splice works on the ORIGINAL Uint8Array, so CRLF, the BOM, trailing whitespace and ill-formed sequences all survive byte-identically; overlapping or out-of-range edits throw rather than corrupting output, and zero edits returns the SAME object

Two-stage self-verification before any download is offered: untouched byte ranges reconstructed independently, then the cleaned bytes RE-DECODED and the code-point sequence compared against what the policy predicted — which is the only check that catches a deletion joining two ill-formed fragments into a new character

Web Worker (module) for decode, classification, the bidi pairing stack and the homoglyph pass. Bytes are COPIED not transferred, because the main thread owns the originals and the byte-exactness guarantee depends on it still having them

Committed Unicode 17.0.0 tables generated locally from UnicodeData/Blocks/Scripts/ScriptExtensions/PropertyValueAliases/PropList/DerivedCoreProperties/emoji-data + UTS #39 confusables/intentional/IdentifierStatus, packed as base-36 delta strings and BUNDLED INTO THE JS — 349 KB raw, 70 KB gzipped. Bundling rather than fetching is what makes the strong claim true: the page makes NO network request at all while it works, verifiable in a network inspector, where 'we do not upload your text' is a claim every competitor already makes

Script_Extensions (not Script) for UTS #39 mixed-script resolution — U+0640 ARABIC TATWEEL is Script=Common but scx={Adlm Arab Mand Mani Ougr Phlp Rohg Sogd Syrc Thaa Yezi}, and using Script would let it pass as neutral inside a Latin string

Two homoglyph gates, because one cannot see the canonical attack: mixed-script tokens (Japanese/Chinese/Korean mixes allowlisted per the Highly Restrictive profile), AND whole-script tokens whose TR39 skeleton is pure ASCII — аррӏе is five-for-five Cyrillic and mixes nothing. Display uses a single-character ASCII fold, never the skeleton, because TR39 maps m to rn and 'apple.corn' reads as a bug rather than a warning

Bidi pairing stack (the GCC -Wbidi-chars=unpaired check), explicitly NOT the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm and labelled as such — plus a two-pane comparison where logical order is produced by substituting every control for a visible token BEFORE insertion, so no reordering can occur and the browser renders logical order for free with no UAX #9 implementation behind it

Intl.Segmenter at grapheme granularity in the reveal pane — a cluster carrying a flagged code point renders INTACT with markers beside it, so an emoji sequence stays one emoji and a Persian word keeps its cursive joins. Splicing a marker into a cluster performs, on legitimate text, exactly the damage the tool warns about

pdfjs-dist 6 getOperatorList with a q/Q graphics-state stack: render mode 3 and 7, ExtGState ca:0 (invisible at mode 0, which a mode-only check misses entirely), and near-white fill — noting pdf.js normalises setFillGray/setFillCMYKColor/setFillColor into setFillRGBColor with a CSS hex STRING, never three floats, and never emits showSpacedText at all. Self-hosted worker via new URL(...) so no CDN appears in the CSP; the whole classifier is a pure function over a synthetic op list and is unit-tested without loading pdf.js

DOMParser HTML pass for text hidden by CSS, with the user's stylesheet parsed as TEXT and @import/url() stripped before anything runs — injecting it to read computed styles would let an untrusted saved page restyle charsight's own interface, including re-triggering the [hidden] display-override trap, and would hand that CSS a network capability

fflate — ONE charsight-run.zip per run, because Safari silently suppresses every programmatic download after the first in a single gesture and a four-download flow hands an iPhone user one file and no error

Four-way overlay dismissal on all four modals and the drawer, verified at 375px with real touch-type PointerEvents rather than .click() — 33 assertions including the [hidden] baseline and elementFromPoint at the viewport centre

File API + drag-and-drop + a real <input type=file>, with looped readEntries (it returns at most 100 at a time and says nothing when it stops) and webkitdirectory FEATURE-DETECTED — iOS Safari has no folder picker, so the button is removed and replaced by a sentence rather than silently degrading to a single-file sheet
WTF-8 encoding on the paste path, so an unpaired surrogate reaches the scanner instead of being rewritten to U+FFFD by TextEncoder and then reported at a position the user never typed

Web Share (level 2, files) + Clipboard + localStorage for the THEME AND PROFILE NAME ONLY — the per-code-point override map is never persisted, because its keys are the exact set of unusual code points found in a document the user scanned precisely because they did not trust it
Service Worker (vite-plugin-pwa; installable, offline app shell with the pdf.js worker and the sample precached — 28 entries, manifest verified rather than assumed)

tools.name: toolwright
tools.description: Paste an agent tool belt and see which provider will reject it, then take the fixed files. Adversarial research refuted ELEVEN load-bearing claims in the original spec, including its headline, and every one changed the build. (1) THE HEADLINE WAS FALSE. post-parse-checks.ts was justified by 'pattern, minLength, minimum, uniqueItems, which strict mode silently lets through' — wrong on all four: pattern and minimum have been on OpenAI's supported list since the 2025-05-20 changelog, and uniqueItems returns a literal 400. The file now rests on four real gaps instead: `strict` omitted or silently falling back to non-strict best-effort (the loudest rule in the product), the GBNF path's per-node drops, oneOf exclusivity that every constrained decoder relaxes to anyOf, and refusal/truncation — plus Anthropic's enum capitalisation, the only documented case in the whole matrix of a provider returning a schema-violating value with a 200 and no signal. (2) 'THREE PROVIDERS' IS A FICTION: the tool SHAPE and the accepted keyword subset vary independently, so eleven targets ship, not three — including OpenAI Responses vs Chat (different envelope AND different error param path), Anthropic strict vs non-strict vs the SDK path that rewrites your schema before sending it, and Gemini's two mutually exclusive schema fields. (3) `strict:false` IS NOT AN ESCAPE HATCH — the Responses API validates the keyword subset regardless, and one bad tool 400s the ENTIRE tools array. (4) THE TRAVERSAL MUST RECURSE: the 2026 Responses array carries type:'namespace' groups the API validates inside, reporting on tools[9].tools[4].parameters, so a flat linter gives a 400ing belt a clean bill of health. (5) THE GBNF DROP LIST WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — llama.cpp DOES enforce pattern, min/maxLength, min/maxItems and integer bounds; what it drops is a different list, and half the drops are CONDITIONAL on sibling keywords, so the drop set is computed per node and that computation is the product. (6) THE PORT IS ~700 LINES, NOT 300, with no JS reference surviving upstream and build_min_max_int requiring BigInt (int64 sentinels; `number` corrupts any bound above 2^53). (7) DO NOT FETCH REMOTE $refs — llama.cpp's C++ passes a stub fetcher, so implementing it would break the CSP AND make the tool disagree with llama-server. (8) THE VALIDATOR DEFAULTS ARE UNSAFE: new Validator() defaults to draft 2019-09 and shortCircuit=true, and the 2020-12 meta-schema CANNOT be used at all because cfworker has zero $dynamicRef implementation and that meta-schema recurses exclusively through it — measured, five nested-error cases all returned valid:true. Draft-07 (4,979 B, self-contained) caught all five. (9) BOTH TOKENIZERS CUT: Anthropic and Gemini have no client-side tokenizer, so two of three columns would be fabrications; gpt-tokenizer/functionCalling speaks only the legacy 2023 functions[] dialect and returns a wrong number for the modern tools[] shape WITH NO ERROR; and the chunk is ~1.0 MB gzipped and silently exceeds workbox's precache cap. Cutting both is what buys 'nothing leaves the tab' — VERIFIED in the browser: analysing a 14-tool belt issues zero network requests. (10) jsonrepair is a good object-literal repairer and a bad truncation detector — it turns {"a":1,"b":[1,2 into valid JSON and a belt truncated mid-key into a fabricated value — so a first-party balance scan runs FIRST and REFUSES rather than repairs. (11) Anthropic DOES publish limits (20 strict tools / 24 optional params / 16 union-typed params) and they are REQUEST-WIDE AGGREGATES, so a 40-tool MCP paste can never be all-strict there. The GBNF port is validated byte-for-byte against llama.cpp's own corpus: 73/73 SUCCESS cases exact, no skips and no loosened comparisons, with the corpus extracted at a pinned commit and committed so CI never touches the network. 188 of 689 matrix cells read UNKNOWN because that is what the documentation supports; the UI says so in words rather than showing a green check. No live provider API call was made to build any rule — every one carries a DOC/SDK/SRC/FIELD provenance badge.
browser_apis: Web Worker (module) that RETAINS the parsed belt — ticking a target recomputes from memory rather than re-parsing, which is what makes an eleven-column matrix feel like a control rather than a report

First-party ~700-line TypeScript port of llama.cpp's common/json-schema-to-grammar.cpp pinned to commit 2f56fc3431f47fe042bf3825e4d5523bdddda993, validated BYTE-FOR-BYTE against llama.cpp's own 75-case test corpus (73 SUCCESS all exact, 2 FAILURE erroring correctly) extracted by a build-time script and committed. Traps the port had to survive: rules sort by BYTE order so digits precede A-Z precedes a-z and `root` is not first (bare .sort(), never localeCompare); `space` placement is a per-construct table and one shared helper for <name>-kv and additional-kv is byte-wrong; absent-or-false additionalProperties means a CLOSED object, the opposite of JSON Schema's default; a property named "" claims the root rule and pushes the object rule to root0; format:uuid emits no node-named rule while date/time/date-time do

Per-node conditional drop computation (this IS the product): minLength/maxLength only when type is exactly "string" and unshadowed by a pattern/enum/const/format sibling; numeric bounds only when type is exactly "integer" (dropped on "number", with a literal TODO in the upstream source); minItems/maxItems dropped on a prefixItems tuple; every keyword sibling to $ref or to oneOf/anyOf silenced by the branch ladder

First-party RFC 4180 CSV writer — control characters become visible escapes so one finding is always one physical line, `;` forces quoting for de/fr/es Excel, formula-injection guard on =+-@ leads, UTF-8 BOM and CRLF

Generated post-parse-checks.ts as a DECLARATIVE TABLE plus a small generic runtime with no imports and no TODOs — a path walker that fans out at every array, and which abstains (as a comment) on nodes inside a union branch rather than emitting a wrong accessor

tools.name: backslide
tools.description: Drop yesterday's eval run and today's and get back only the rows that got worse, with the reason attached. Adversarial review found nine blockers and every one changed the build, so the shipped design inverts the spec in several places. (1) THE SPECIFIED JSON CLASSIFIER IS WRONG IN THREE DIRECTIONS. `jsonrepair` 3.15.0 THROWS on "Sure! Here's the JSON:" — the apostrophe in "Here's" is read as an opening quote, so the single most common wrapper case is misfiled; it SUCCEEDS on `{"a":1,"b":[1,2` , silently closing the brackets so a max-tokens cut-off would be reported as "structurally sound", which is the opposite of the truth about the most consequential regression there is; and it turns "I cannot help with that." into a valid JSON string, so a refusal reads as valid JSON. A first-party structural classifier ships instead (largest balanced span, string-and-escape aware) returning valid|wrapper|truncated|prose|malformed, and jsonrepair is not a dependency at all. (2) THE SCORERS ARE NOT DISJOINT AND THE HEADLINE DOUBLE-COUNTED. An errored row has an empty output, `JSON.parse('')` throws, so a run that hit a 429 storm would read "300 of them stopped returning valid JSON" and send the user to debug a formatting bug that does not exist. Strict precedence now gives the first applicable check ownership of a row and marks the rest not-counted, which is what makes the per-check column sum to the regression total — and what allows the headline to be GENERATED from the summary rather than transcribed. The measured sample reads 20 regressions / 16 is-json / 4 schema / 5 errored reported separately; the idea file's hand-written "14" was wrong. (3) js-rouge WAS CUT ENTIRELY: it throws RangeError on the empty strings that are exactly the interesting rows, scores identical text 0.833 because its intersection is set-based (0.44 on identical JSON), has no ESM default export, promptfoo lowercases before calling it so the parity argument is false — and on a harmless paraphrase ROUGE-L drops 0.50, five times any threshold, flagging precisely what the tool exists not to flag. (4) THE FUZZY JOIN NEEDS NO MODEL: an affix-stripped hash join scores 300/300 in 1.63 ms, and the only failures are byte-identical inputs, which embeddings tie on identically — so the specified static-embedding column was dropped, removing the collision with searchpack (same model, two days earlier) and loraprep (same ORT+WebGPU shape, same day). (5) EVERY ID-BASED DIALECT KEYS ON A POSITION — testIdx, data_source_idx, oaieval's trailing ordinal — so inserting three test cases at the top of a config makes every row join to the wrong partner at 100% coverage stamped 'exact'. The key join is now VERIFIED against the inputs (how many identical inputs the files share vs how many the ids lined up) and thrown away when they disagree; a similarity median cannot catch this because formulaic inputs are 90% alike. (6) FANOUT IDENTITY CANNOT CONTAIN THE PROMPT TEXT: changing one line of the prompt is the tool's whole premise, and a text-based branch identity makes A's and B's branch sets disjoint so NOTHING is scored and the headline reads '0 rows got worse'. (7) AMBIGUOUS GROUPS ARE A MULTISET, NOT A BIJECTION — the same three-row group reports 1 or 2 regressions depending on which arbitrary pairing is picked, on files whose line order the tool itself calls meaningless. (8) THE MATCHER ABSTAINS: greedy max-weight (never nearest-neighbour, which double-assigned 4 rows; never Hungarian, which force-matches everything) with a MARGIN rather than a level — true paraphrase partners score 0.18-0.42 against impostors at 0.08-0.14, so a fixed 0.55 threshold rejects every real paraphrase. (9) A CAPABILITY CHECK: 'nothing got worse' is only honest when something could look, so a file with no assertions, no reference and no structured output gets 'nothing here can be objectively checked' plus a ranked reading list. Also: @cfworker/json-schema needs BOTH '2020-12' (it defaults to 2019-09) and shortCircuit:false (it defaults true, reporting one error where the product promises 'the reason attached'), and ajv is disqualified outright because it compiles with the Function constructor and dies under the CSP; diffJson must receive PARSED OBJECTS or it degrades to a line diff and reports noise on exactly the key-reorder case it was chosen for; carried assertions are keyed on (type, value, ordinal) or two same-type assertions swapping outcomes fabricate a regression and hide a fix on one row; generic field mapping is resolved JOINTLY over both files or a build that logs an extra long field makes every row flip; and GitHub's sanitiser allows neither <style> nor style=, so the PR artefact is Markdown and the styled HTML is a separate export.
browser_apis: Web Worker (module) that RETAINS the parsed rows — flipping a normalisation rule or a threshold recomputes over memory rather than re-reading, re-transferring or re-parsing, which is what makes the live symbol-alphabet panel feel instant; alignment is microseconds per case so a 300-case recompute lands inside one frame

First-party structural JSON classifier (unit-tested against the real jsonrepair, which is kept as a devDependency purely to pin its three measured defects as regression tests) — walks the raw text respecting string literals and escapes, so braces inside strings and \" escapes cannot fool it

First-party Gotoh affine-gap Needleman-Wunsch over tool-call trajectories (unit-tested): 15 steps with one inserted at index 2 gives `==+=============`, one gap, 15 exact — against 14 differences from a naive index-wise zip, which the test asserts alongside it so the reason the algorithm exists is documented. GAP_OPEN(-4) vs MISMATCH(-2) is load-bearing: two gaps must cost more than one substitution or a tool SWAP is absorbed as delete+insert. An Ix->Iy transition is allowed so a block replacement does not under-report

First-party four-stage join cascade (unit-tested): verified exact-key -> per-file common-affix stripping with a suffix CLAMP (an unclamped slice returns '' for any row shorter than prefix+suffix, inventing an ambiguous group out of empty strings) -> four scored key functions (full / affix / last paragraph / tail-200, scored matched-minus-2x-ambiguous) -> greedy max-weight similarity with abstention
First-party character 3-gram Jaccard with space padding, so strings shorter than n are well defined rather than NaN

@cfworker/json-schema 4.1.1 with BOTH the draft and shortCircuit passed explicitly — the only schema validator that compiles no code, which is the sole reason schema checking is possible under a strict CSP at all

diff 9.0.0 — diffJson on PARSED OBJECTS when both sides parse (0 hunks on key reorder and whitespace reflow), diffWords otherwise; diffArrays deliberately unused since the o200k token-diff it needed was cut at 1,065,794 B gzipped for a view that matched diffWords in 8 of 11 measured cases and was worse in 1
fastest-levenshtein 1.0.16 — Class B only, structurally incapable of producing a verdict

First-party RFC 4180 CSV reader and writer — ragged rows never throw, control characters become visible escapes so one record is always one physical line, formula-injection guard on =+-@ leads, UTF-8 BOM and CRLF for Excel, empty cell (never 0) for a metric the file did not carry

First-party byte-exact strict passthrough — the source line is emitted verbatim with metadata in a sidecar where line n describes line n, because JSON.parse+stringify rounds big integers, turns 1.0 into 1 and drops duplicate keys
Self-contained diff-report.html asserted by test to contain no http://, no https://, no <script, no <link and no src=
Four-way overlay dismissal on every modal and the drawer, verified at 375px with real touch-type PointerEvents rather than .click()
File API + drag-and-drop + a real <input type=file> on both drop zones — iOS Safari cannot drag and drop at all
File System Access / anchor download + Web Share (level 2) + Clipboard + localStorage (theme and thresholds only)
Service Worker (vite-plugin-pwa; installable, offline app shell WITH the samples precached — an offline claim whose only zero-friction entry point 404s offline is not an offline claim)

tools.name: loraprep
tools.description: Turn a folder of photos into a clean, deduplicated LoRA training set — entirely in the browser. Two findings from adversarial verification decided the whole build, and both invert what the idea file specified. (1) THE VISION MODEL IS NEVER ALLOWED TO SET AN IMAGE ASIDE. The obvious design — embed, threshold cosine, union-find, keep one per cluster — was measured against google/dreambooth (158 hand-curated photographs, zero duplicates) and cannot work: different photos of the SAME subject reach cosine 0.9916 (median 0.80, p99 0.97) while true duplicates bottom out at 0.878 mirrored, 0.855 greyscale, 0.726 watermarked. The distributions overlap in the WRONG DIRECTION — at 0.90 you miss flips/rotations/greyscale/crops AND falsely condemn 49 of 342 same-subject pairs; at 0.98 you catch 1 of 13 duplicate families, the one dHash already finds at 1 bit. Union-find was worse: at 0.90 single-linkage collapsed six visually distinct photographs of one bowl into one survivor through a chain scoring 0.809, nine hundredths BELOW the threshold that formed the cluster, taking 35 of 158 images. So the 64-bit dHash (zero false matches across all 12,403 pairs at Hamming<=5) does the automatic part and the model produces ranked PAIRS with nothing pre-selected. (2) THE MODEL FILE THE IDEA SPECIFIED IS NUMERICALLY BROKEN: vision_model_quantized.onnx (11,846,843 B, int8) scores cosine 0.093 against its own fp32 output and gives four unrelated images pairwise cosines of 0.73-0.88 where fp32 gives 0.08-0.17 — every image similar to every other, which would destroy a dataset silently. The repo's own config.json quietly steers around it (transformers.js_config.dtype.vision_model = fp32). Ships fp16 (22,876,479 B, cosine 0.99999) and does not take its own word for it: a boot self-check embeds a code-generated probe and compares against a reference vector committed to the repo, rejecting any backend below 0.985 — which is what makes trying WebGPU first safe (measured 0.99972 live; the broken int8 measures 0.48). Three more measured corrections. SHARPNESS ALONE PICKS THE WORST FILE: variance-of-Laplacian rises as JPEG quality falls (one photo at q92/82/76 scores 40/53/73) so sharpest-wins keeps the most damaged copy; a 3x3 pre-filter does NOT fix it (3.44/5.94/7.24) because blocking is structural, so the keeper rule uses sharpness only to decide what is IN FOCUS (blurred frames score 6-17% of their group best) then prefers the most bytes per pixel, bucketed by powers of two so a real burst still decides on sharpness. DECODE AND INFERENCE MUST NOT SHARE A THREAD: alternating createImageBitmap with session.run degrades inference from 138ms to ~1050ms (7.6x, reproduced in two Chrome builds, partial separation does not help), so a decode-worker pool feeds a separate inference worker — measured 10.6s to 5.0s on the sample. And resizeWidth/resizeHeight on createImageBitmap is a NO-OP or slower in Chromium (338ms vs 285ms full decode), so it is kept for correctness, never quoted as a saving. Also: transformers.js silently points wasmPaths at cdn.jsdelivr.net, overridden to self-hosted /ort/ so the CSP names no CDN and the offline claim is true (verified cold: the cache holds exactly 3 pinned huggingface.co URLs + 2 same-origin files, no text tower, no tokenizer); fflate writes no ZIP64 and silently wraps the central-directory offset above 4 GiB, so the writer refuses with an explanation instead; and every input image appears exactly once in dedup-report.csv, asserted by a partition test.
browser_apis: Web Workers (module) x2 kinds — a decode pool and ONE inference worker that never touches an image decoder. This is the single biggest performance decision: interleaving createImageBitmap with session.run in one loop degrades ORT inference 7.6x (138ms -> 1050ms), measured in Chrome 148 and 150, and chunking 8-and-8 does not help (1037ms) — only full phase separation restores 141ms. The inference worker also carries a watchdog that rebuilds the session (791ms) if it degrades past 2.5x baseline, because a degraded session was observed to stay degraded for a whole run

@huggingface/transformers 4.2.0 with CLIPVisionModelWithProjection.from_pretrained — NOT the pipeline API: the pipeline returns `last_hidden_state ?? logits ?? image_embeds`, so an export that also emits patch tokens silently hands back [1,N,768] instead of the projected [1,512]. The class hard-defaults model_file_name to 'vision_model', so the 42.8 MB text tower and the 2.2 MB tokenizer are never fetched (verified by inspecting the browser cache after a cold run)
dtype ALWAYS passed explicitly — transformers.js has DEFAULT_DEVICE_DTYPE_MAPPING = { wasm: 'q8' }, so omitting it on the WASM device silently loads the broken int8 export

WebGPU first, WASM fallback, each gated on a boot self-check against a committed fp32 reference vector — the only defensible way to offer a backend that can return plausible-but-wrong numbers. GitHub Pages cannot set COOP/COEP, so ORT silently sets numThreads=1; that is surfaced in the UI rather than hidden

Self-hosted onnxruntime-web WASM binaries (public/ort/, copied from node_modules at build time, gitignored) — transformers.js otherwise sets wasmPaths to cdn.jsdelivr.net on import. The ORT base URL is resolved on the MAIN thread from document.baseURI and passed in, because import.meta.env.BASE_URL inside a worker resolves against the worker's own /assets/ path and ORT then fails with 'no available backend found'
A Vite plugin that DELETES the dead 23.5 MB ort-wasm-*.wasm asset Vite emits from ORT's `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` — it is never fetched, because wasmPaths points elsewhere

createImageBitmap + OffscreenCanvas + getImageData — decode once to a fixed square 256x256 grid, close() immediately; the final 256->9x8 reduction is a first-party box filter, NOT the browser's resizer, because resizeQuality 'low' vs 'high' moves the hash by up to 21 bits on hard-edged content and would make duplicate detection browser-dependent
Transferable ArrayBuffers — 256 KB pixel buffers cross workers without copying; the queue is the backpressure, so decoded frames cannot pile up ahead of inference

First-party dHash-64 (unit-tested) matching imagehash's polarity (right > left) so the hex in the report is comparable with a Python cross-check; measured through a real browser decode: JPEG q40 = 1 bit, 25% resize = 1, 6px blur = 1, 5% crop = 14, MIRROR FLIP = 30, 90-degree rotation = 31 against 31 for an unrelated photograph — mirrored copies are not merely hard to find, they are indistinguishable from random, and the UI says so

First-party variance-of-Laplacian + flatness (unit-tested) — used ONLY to decide what is in focus within a group, never as an absolute blur verdict, because the measure scales with resolution, content AND compression
First-party union-find with iterative path compression over dHash edges only (unit-tested incl. a 20,000-deep chain), with the single-linkage caveat disclosed in the UI rather than buried

First-party image-header parser for JPEG/PNG/WebP(3 variants)/GIF/BMP (unit-tested against REAL ImageMagick-generated files incl. a progressive JPEG behind SOF2 and a 20 KB EXIF block) — reads true pixel dimensions from 256 KB of header so the pipeline never needs a second full-resolution decode

First-party streaming ZIP over fflate ZipPassThrough (STORED, method 0 — deflate saves 0.04% on camera JPEGs for 7.4x the CPU) with a hard refusal above 3.9 GB and 65,000 entries, because fflate emits no ZIP64 and silently wraps the central-directory offset mod 2^32 above 4 GiB. Verified by a test that runs the SYSTEM unzip against the output, since the streaming writer uses data descriptors and the local headers all read zero

File System Access API (showSaveFilePicker + createWritable, where the awaited write IS the backpressure; showDirectoryPicker to read) with an explicitly capped in-memory Blob fallback — Chromium documents 2 GB on desktop but total_physical_memory/100 on Android

DataTransferItem.webkitGetAsEntry with a LOOPED readEntries (it returns at most 100 at a time, so the naive single call silently truncates a 3,000-photo folder to 100), plus <input webkitdirectory> and a dropped .zip as first-class fallbacks

First-party path-safety for every ZIP entry name (unit-tested): separators, control bytes, Windows reserved names, trailing dots and every run of dots collapsed — a hostile archive's `../../.ssh/authorized_keys` must not survive into the output the user extracts

kohya_ss/sd-scripts layout read from the trainers' own source: the <repeats>_<class> folder is parsed by split('_'), a top-level wrapper folder is REQUIRED, glob_images is non-recursive, captions are read with lines[0].strip() so they are collapsed to one line, and UTF-8 WITHOUT BOM because Python's utf-8 codec leaves U+FEFF glued to the trigger word. metadata.jsonl carries the caption under BOTH `text` and `prompt` because diffusers has no single convention
Cache API — the model is stored after the first run and the tool then works offline
Web Share API (level 2, files) + Clipboard API + localStorage (theme only)
Service Worker (vite-plugin-pwa; installable, offline app shell + sample precached, ORT binaries and the model deliberately excluded from precache)

tools.name: scrubjay
tools.description: Scan a training or eval dataset for live-shaped API keys and personal data before it leaves your machine, and get back a pseudonymised copy that still trains plus an encrypted mapping only you can reverse. It exists because every hosted scanner has the same absurdity at its heart: uploading the file to learn whether the file is safe to upload IS the disclosure. 27 recognisers on by default out of 29 — 4 checksum-validated (Luhn, IBAN mod-97, ABA 3-7-1, SSN structural exclusion), 19 published provider prefixes, 4 structural, and 2 heuristics that ship SWITCHED OFF because a scanner that cries wolf gets turned off and a scanner that gets turned off protects nobody. Three decisions carry the build. (1) TWO SPANS PER FINDING, always: overlap resolution uses the whole match, redaction uses the capture group, and they differ on five rules — redacting match[0] on url-embedded-credential destroys the scheme, user and host of a DSN, and a pem-private-key rule that matches only the header redacts 30 characters and leaves the entire key body in the file you are calling clean, which is the worst failure this product can have (a test asserts that span exceeds 78 chars). (2) IT NEVER PARSES YOUR JSON: JSON.parse -> JSON.stringify turns 12345678901234567890 into ...67000, 1.0 into 1, and drops duplicate keys, while TextDecoder substitutes U+FFFD over the invalid UTF-8 that real multi-GB exports contain — so detection decodes a COPY and the splice works on the original bytes, with spliceBytes(raw, []) returning the same object. (3) GZIP GOES THROUGH FFLATE, NOT DecompressionStream, at a measured 2.26x cost, because `cat shard-00.gz shard-01.gz` is routine in sharded pipelines, browser multi-member behaviour is unverified, and the gzip ISIZE check is UNSOUND on it (equal shards make a truncated read pass) — silently scanning half a file and reporting clean is the worst outcome available. The entropy heuristic was redesigned after measurement killed the obvious version: H >= 3.5 bits/char flags English prose (4.53) and git SHAs (3.91) while MISSING real 20-char hex secrets (mean 3.36), because max entropy at length L is log2(L) and a constant bits/char gate is length-coupled by construction; what ships is length-normalised eta = H/log2(alphabet) at 0.92, behind an unbounded candidate tokeniser and ten structural suppressors — and it is still off by default. Pseudonyms are HMAC-SHA256 folded to 50 bits in Crockford base32; the sketched PERSON_0f3a (16 bits) was unshippable at a 50% collision point of 301 values. Triage is keyboard-first on ONE verb: unreviewed means redacted, so triage only lets you un-redact what it got wrong. Honest limits are stated first, not buried: no personal names and no postal addresses (GLiNER cut at 192 MB), a checksum rules out a typo not a coincidence (~1 in 10 random nine-digit strings passes ABA, asserted in the suite because the UI prints it), US SSNs have had no checksum since 2011 so an order number like 192-83-7465 does match, and a clean report means nothing matched rather than that the file is clean. Two real bugs were caught by the browser dry-run rather than by unit tests: a self-referential `await writeChain` inside a .then() on writeChain that deadlocked every run at 100%, and an idempotence break where the unquoted branch of generic-secret-assignment re-matched its own [REDACTED:...] marker because ] sits outside its character class.
browser_apis: File.stream() + ReadableStream — multi-GB streaming with no upload; .getReader() and a while loop, NEVER `for await...of` a ReadableStream (async stream iteration is Safari 27, i.e. essentially no iPhone in the field)
Web Workers (module) + MessageChannel — a reader worker owns the bytes end to end and talks to N scanner workers over private ports, so the main thread never touches the hot path

Transferable ArrayBuffer with COUNT-based credits — the credits ARE the backpressure, so the reader physically cannot allocate ahead of the pool; resident memory is exactly workers x 2 x chunkBytes (64 MiB desktop, 6 MiB mobile) at any file size. Credits are a count rather than a recycled buffer because in pass 2 the splicer returns the SAME buffer when a chunk is clean, so it cannot simultaneously be the output and the credit. No SharedArrayBuffer, hence no COOP/COEP, hence it runs on GitHub Pages unmodified

Web Crypto HMAC-SHA256 — stable pseudonyms (same email always the same token) folded to 50 bits of Crockford base32, memoised per worker because a non-extractable CryptoKey means one subtle.sign per distinct value

Web Crypto PBKDF2 (600,000 rounds, the current OWASP figure) + AES-GCM-256 — the mapping container, with an explicit key commitment because AES-GCM is not key-committing (Albertini et al., USENIX 2022). The wrong-passphrase and altered-header cases are DELIBERATELY reported with one combined message, because prk = f(passphrase, salt, iterations) means the commitment shadows the AAD for exactly the header fields AAD protects — a test asserts the combined string verbatim so nobody 'fixes' it into a false promise

First-party position-preserving JSON string scanner (unit-tested) — walks raw bytes and returns each string literal with an RFC 6901 pointer plus a decoded-index -> byte-offset map, so a value like "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----\nMIIEow\u002FABC" (10 decoded chars over 15 raw bytes) splices at the right byte

First-party byte splicer (unit-tested) — spliceBytes(raw, []) returns the same object with zero copies; overlapping and out-of-range edits throw rather than corrupting output; invalid UTF-8, big integers, 1.0, 1e5 and duplicate keys all survive byte-identically

First-party recogniser registry (29 rules, every pattern carrying the `d` flag, asserted by test) with two independent spans per finding and a published does-not-match line per rule rendered in the preflight UI

First-party validators (unit-tested): Luhn, IBAN mod-97 with a SWIFT length table, ABA 3-7-1, three-valued SSN structural exclusion (never a boolean — a `=== true` caller silently dropped every known-invalid plant during design), and jwtDecodable implemented against atob NOT Buffer.from, because Buffer is lenient and would accept 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9!!!' in Node while the browser throws

First-party length-normalised entropy gate with ten structural suppressors (hex-digest case-insensitively incl. 48, uuid, iso8601, semver, media-b64 magic prefixes, path, single-class, wordy, plus scrubjay's own pseudonym and redaction-marker forms for idempotence) — candidate extraction is UNBOUNDED at the top end because a {24,512} cap splits a 1400-char base64 blob into pieces and the 376-char tail then fires

First-party overlap resolver (unit-tested) — lower tier wins, spans are half-open so adjacent findings both survive, suppressed findings are RETAINED because the triage kill-count and the context projection both need them, and a rule-name tiebreak makes output a deterministic function of input (which is what makes a golden-file test possible)

First-party context projection — the 40-char window is computed from the FULLY redacted text with post-redaction offsets and every candidate span applied, so a dismissed high-entropy blob next to a reported email cannot walk into findings.csv in plaintext; surrogate pairs are clamped explicitly because String.prototype.at is not code-point aware

First-party RFC 4180 CSV writer — control chars become visible escapes so one finding is always one physical line (deliberate deviation: a findings.csv whose row count differs from its line count cannot be wc -l'd or grep'd), `;` triggers quoting for de/fr/es Excel locales, leading =/+/-/@ gets a formula-injection prefix, UTF-8 BOM, CRLF, and JSON pointers have PII-shaped object keys masked because the path column leaks on its own
fflate Gunzip — multi-member-correct gzip input, chosen over DecompressionStream at a measured 2.26x cost because the ISIZE trailer check is unsound on concatenated members
CompressionStream('gzip') — optional gzip output, defaulted OFF because compression runs at roughly a twelfth of read speed

hyparquet 1.27.1 + hyparquet-compressors — Parquet read one row group at a time in 262 KB of pure JS instead of a 150 MB DuckDB bundle; the largest row group is computed from the footer and printed BEFORE the scan, because 'nothing lands in memory' is false on that path

File System Access API (showSaveFilePicker + createWritable, where the awaited write IS the backpressure) — mode:'exclusive' deliberately unused because it is Chrome 121+ only and writes in place, so a tab crash leaves a truncated file that looks complete. Falls back to an in-memory Blob hard-capped at 512 MiB, then findings-only, with the branch and its ceiling stated in preflight

Crockford base32 project key (unit-tested exhaustively over 1,260 single-character substitutions: zero silently produced a DIFFERENT key; the handful that validate are documented O/0 and I/L/1 folds decoding to the identical key, which a 20-bit checksum cannot reject by construction)

Rejection-sampled passphrase (9 words from a 390-word list = 77.5 bits; 6 words would be 51.6 and is not enough against a GPU at 600k PBKDF2 rounds), with NO auto-copy to clipboard because Universal Clipboard and Windows Cloud Clipboard sync it between devices
Four-way overlay dismissal on every modal and the drawer (x control, backdrop pointerdown, Escape, outside-panel pointer), verified at 375px with real touch-type PointerEvents rather than .click()
Service Worker (vite-plugin-pwa; installable, offline app shell + precached sample)

tools.name: searchpack
tools.description: Point it at a folder of docs and it builds a semantic search engine on your own machine — a binary index, a subsetted embedding table and a dependency-free search.js, zipped. Unpack it into your site's public/ and you have search: no account, no vector database, no per-query cost, nothing hosted. The engine then runs on your READERS' machines, so nobody's queries reach anyone, including you. The idea that makes it possible: sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 is not really a neural network — its entire ONNX graph is Gather(table, ids) -> DequantizeLinear -> ReduceMean, so an embedding is the average of one uint8 table row per word piece. Searchpack therefore skips ONNX Runtime completely: a ~200-line protobuf reader lifts the uint8[30522,1024] table out by name, and the averaging happens in plain JS. That is the only reason a search engine can be handed to a third party at all — 26 KB of JS instead of 11 MB of WASM. The per-tensor scale (1.2497) factors out of the mean and is annihilated by L2 normalisation, so only zero_point=121 is needed. Three findings from adversarial review changed the build. (1) sentence-transformers calls encode_batch(add_special_tokens=False), so adding [CLS]/[SEP] 'to match the reference' is the DEVIATION — it moves a one-word query by cosine 0.24. (2) Subsetting the TOKENIZER vocabulary is the obvious optimisation and is wrong: WordPiece is greedy longest-match, so removing entries re-segments unknown words rather than silencing them — 41% of held-out words become in-index pieces, and a search for 'carpet' would confidently retrieve every page about CARS. So all 30,522 token strings ship (~230 KB) and only the ~1,000 embedding rows the corpus touches are subsetted, applied as a post-filter. (3) Plain mean-pooling is dominated by function words: 'how do I stop it retrying forever' scored 0.03 and ranked an unrelated page first; IDF-weighted pooling using document frequencies computed from the user's OWN corpus takes it to 0.46 and ranks correctly, at one float per shipped row. Retrieval is three modes in the shipped shim — semantic (256-bit binary-code Hamming pre-pass via counting sort, then exact int8 cosine rescore), Okapi BM25 over the same word pieces, and reciprocal-rank-fusion hybrid (the default, because pooled embeddings are weakest on exactly what docs search gets most: identifiers, flags, error codes). The pack verifies itself before download: the EMITTED search.js is loaded from a Blob URL and run against the EMITTED binaries — round-trip cosine 1.000000 across 20 chunks, exact because the tokenizer and engine are literally the same source files in both places (?raw imports of src/shim/*.runtime.js); binary pre-pass kept 100% of exhaustive results; a failing pack is still emitted, labelled 'unverified'. HTML extraction is first-party rather than Readability precisely because Readability discards the heading ids a docs search needs to deep-link. Honest limit stated in the UI, not buried: static embeddings score ~35 on MTEB Retrieval vs ~43 for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and ~52 for bge-small; measured on the bundled 18-page sample, five conversational questions phrased to avoid the answering page's wording put the right page in the top three TWICE. English only. Nothing you select ever leaves the tab; the sole network call is one anonymous pinned GET of the public model, cached for offline use. Generated packs are released under MIT (not AGPL) so users can ship them on their own sites.
browser_apis: First-party ONNX protobuf reader (~200 lines, no ONNX Runtime, no WASM): walks ModelProto -> graph -> initializers AND node-attribute subgraphs, locating embedding.weight_quantized BY NAME rather than by hardcoded offset; reads scale from float_data (field 4) and zero_point from int32_data (field 5), NOT raw_data — a raw_data-only reader silently returns garbage (measured cosine 0.0046 vs 0.9999); hard-rejects a QInt8 re-export rather than mis-decoding it, and explains itself when weights live in an external .onnx_data file

First-party WordPiece tokenizer verified byte-for-byte against HuggingFace on 39 committed fixture cases: BertNormalizer (clean_text -> handle_chinese_chars -> strip accents -> lowercase, in that order because strip_accents:null follows lowercase and runs BEFORE it) + BertPreTokenizer + greedy longest-match with whole-word [UNK] collapse. Two real bugs it caught: JavaScript's \s matches U+FEFF but Rust's is_whitespace does not, so format characters must be filtered BEFORE the whitespace fold or a BOM splits a word; and max_input_chars_per_word is counted in CODE POINTS, so 60 astral emoji (120 UTF-16 units) must not trip the 100-character gate

The shared-runtime trick: src/shim/*.runtime.js are plain dependency-free JS with hand-written .d.ts siblings; the app imports them normally and the packer imports the SAME FILES with Vite's ?raw suffix and concatenates their literal source into the emitted search.js — so build-time embedder and shipped shim agree BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by discipline (round-trip cosine measured at exactly 1.000000)

First-party IDF-weighted pooling (unit-tested): embedding = normalize(SUM idf(t) * (row[t] - zeroPoint)), with idf computed from the user's own corpus in a first tokenization pass, floored so a ubiquitous token contributes a trace rather than vanishing; also gives a principled 'no signal' test — a nonsense query whose summed weight falls below a floor returns nothing instead of ten arbitrary neighbours (nonsense does NOT become [UNK]: bert-base-uncased has every letter, so 'zzqqxwv' shatters into ubiquitous single-character subwords)

First-party binary formats (unit-tested round-trip incl. alignment): vocab.bin = all token strings + u16 rowIndex filter + f32 IDF weights + the subsetted uint8 rows; index.bin = 256-bit binary codes + int8 vectors + f32 norms + BM25 postings + metadata JSON, with every typed-array view kept 4-byte aligned by explicit padding

First-party two-stage semantic retrieval: Hamming distance over 32x-smaller binary codes selected by a COUNTING SORT over the distance range (no comparison sort), then exact int8 cosine rescore of candidates only; int8 quantisation scale cancels because the stored int8 norm is the divisor

tools.name: chatprint
tools.description: See the literal string your model actually receives. Paste the request body your code was about to send and chatprint renders it through the model's OWN Jinja chat template, tokenizes it with the model's OWN tokenizer, and attributes every token to a segment — system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents, each turn, template overhead — then packs it down to a budget. It exists because the two things that eat a context window (tool definitions and retrieved documents) are precisely the two you never see. The headline finding is measured, not asserted: the same 20-message sample costs 6,478 tokens on Granite 3.3, 6,237 on Qwen2.5, 6,119 on Llama 3.1 and 1,900 on Phi-3.5 — because four of the ten templates tested SILENTLY IGNORE the tools array, so those models would never know the tools exist. The second is that Llama 3.2's own template injects the current date near the start of the prompt, so the identical request rendered a day later shares only a 24-token prefix out of 6,119: its template destroys 99.6% of your prompt cache every day with no help from your code. Attribution is the hard part and is done by LOCATING rather than counting: tokenizing messages separately is out by +23/-60 on a 53-token prompt, and subtracting consecutive prefix counts is also wrong because Phi-3.5 appends eos_token when add_generation_prompt is false. Instead every cut point is found by longest-common-TOKEN-prefix against the one ground-truth token array, so spans tile [0,total) and the column sums to the truth by construction. Two guards came from real bugs caught during the build: prefixes must be rendered WITH the tools (Llama splices them into the first USER message, and rendering prefixes without them collapsed every cut onto the final turn while still summing exactly), and a separate degeneracy check hides a breakdown where one segment holds >90% of tokens — because the sum invariant cannot catch that class of failure. Also caught: encode() applies the post-processor and adds a SECOND beginning-of-text token on Llama and Mistral because the template already wrote one, so every count uses add_special_tokens:false. Artefacts: rendered-prompt.txt (byte-exact), token-budget.csv (one column per model compared) and messages.trimmed.json (packed to fit, never orphaning a tool result from its call, never silently dropping the system prompt, always keeping the final turn). Honesty is enforced in the UI: Claude is labelled ESTIMATE inline and never default-selected because no public local tokenizer exists after Claude 3, with Anthropic's free count_tokens endpoint named as the exact alternative; OpenAI rows are labelled as OpenAI's documented per-message accounting rather than a byte-exact render; gated repos (meta-llama, google/gemma, all Cohere) are absent because they 401 anonymously, and faithful community mirrors are badged 'mirror'. Nothing you paste leaves the tab — the only network request is an anonymous GET of a public tokenizer file, listed in the event log. Installable PWA, offline after the first tokenizer download.

tools.name: ggufscope
tools.description: Will this GGUF fit on your GPU? Paste a Hugging Face repo id (or drop a local .gguf) and GGUFScope reads the model's REAL tensor table straight out of the file with a single HTTP Range request — about 8 MB of a multi-gigabyte model, ~0.1% of it — then computes exactly what it needs in VRAM. It exists because the SEO 'VRAM calculator' pages guess from a parameter count and a quant name, and both inputs are unreliable: Q4_K_M is a llama-quantize MIXTURE (attention V, the FFN down projection and the output head are stored at higher precision, and a row length not divisible by the block size silently falls back to another type — qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf is 133 Q5_0 tensors and only 12 Q4_K, a true 6.16 bpw vs the assumed 4.85), and the KV cache depends on GQA geometry a parameter count cannot reveal (Qwen3-32B declares key_length 128 while 5120/64 = 80, an 8192 vs 5120 MiB error at 32k that says a model fits when it does not). Weight bytes come from ggml's real block sizes; the KV cache reproduces llama.cpp's own per-layer formula including explicit key_length/value_length, per-layer head_count_kv and the 256-token context padding. The killer assertion is a self-check: the summed tensor table is reconciled against the file's true size read from Content-Range — exact match shows 'verified', a mismatch is surfaced rather than hidden, which catches fork quantisations, removed ggml types and truncated downloads for free (delta 0 bytes on every model tested). Solvers find the largest -ngl and the largest context that fit. Sharded models are fully supported (shards 2+ are ~10 KB each). Artefacts: fit-report.json, a solved llama-server command line (which forces -fa on whenever the KV cache is quantised, because llama.cpp exits otherwise), an Ollama Modelfile, chat_template.jinja rendered live, and a 1200x630 report-card PNG. A local .gguf is read with Blob.slice and never uploaded; remote inspection is honestly disclosed as a request to Hugging Face. Working memory is shown as an adjustable allowance, never folded silently into the headline, because llama.cpp's compute buffer has no closed form; MLA and sliding-window models are flagged as upper bounds. KV figures are checked in CI against numbers llama.cpp itself printed at startup.

Guard against a server that ignores Range and answers 200: the body is stream-read to the requested length and then cancelled, so the tool never downloads the model it exists to avoid downloading

First-party GGUF binary parser (DataView + TextDecoder, little- and big-endian): magic/version/counts, the full metadata KV block, and the tensor-info table; throws NeedMoreBytes on a truncated prefix rather than yielding zero-shaped tensors, which is the failure mode that would silently report 0 GB

Progressive Range ladder (8 MB → 24 MB → 64 MB → 160 MB): the tensor table sits AFTER all metadata, and the tokenizer vocabulary is in that metadata, so real headers start 5.7–7.5 MB in (measured: Qwen3-8B 5.68 MB, Llama-3.2-1B 7.47 MB, gemma-3-4b 6.24 MB, Qwen3-32B 5.70 MB) — one request covers the overwhelming majority

tools.name: tiltwell
tools.description: A spirit level, angle finder, inclinometer and roof-pitch meter in your browser — it turns the phone's orientation sensor into a precise 2-axis bubble level and a clinometer, then hands you the number as a saved measurement, a CSV and a report card. tools.name: burnwell
tools.description: A one-time, burn-after-read secret sender — hand a password, API key or recovery phrase straight from your browser to the recipient's over a direct WebRTC data channel (DTLS on the wire), additionally sealed in AES-GCM-256 with a key derived from the room passphrase, so the plaintext exists only inside the two tabs. Unlike the paste-into-a-website services, NOTHING is ever stored on a server, encrypted or otherwise: the secret only moves while both people are connected, and it's released to exactly one verified recipient (the first to reveal it) then burned — wiped from the sender's tab and the room torn down; a second device that opens the link afterwards gets 'already delivered'. Peer discovery + signalling ride public nostr relays via trystero, with the handshake encrypted by the passphrase so a relay sees only ciphertext; a four-word Short Authentication String catches a MITM relay. Two link modes: full link (passphrase in the hash) or split (link carries only the room; the four-word passphrase is read aloud out-of-band, so the link alone can't open the secret). The one-time-delivery rule is a pure, exhaustively unit-tested state machine. Takeaway artefacts: the recipient copies the revealed secret; the sender gets a 'delivered & burned' receipt. Honest limitation stated in the Threat Model: both parties must be online at once (the price of never storing anything), and one static key from the passphrase (no forward secrecy).
